title: 04. BM25 & Lexical Search: Vector Space Model — TF-IDF & Cosine Similarity
summary: The Vector Space Model (VSM) represents documents and queries as vectors in a high-dimensional term space (one dimension per unique vocabulary term). Each dimension's value is the TF-IDF weight of the corresponding term.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body:
The Vector Space Model (VSM) represents documents and queries as vectors in a high-dimensional term space (one dimension per unique vocabulary term). Each dimension's value is the TF-IDF weight of the corresponding term. Relevance is measured as cosine similarity between the query vector and each document vector, making it scale-invariant with respect to document length. VSM enables ranking (unlike Boolean), supports partial matching, and is geometrically interpretable. The key insight is that documents and queries occupy the same vector space, and angular proximity implies topical similarity.

$$\text{cosine}(q, d) = \frac{q \cdot d}{|q| \cdot |d|} = \frac{\sum_{t} w_{t,q} \cdot w_{t,d}}{\sqrt{\sum_t w_{t,q}^2} \cdot \sqrt{\sum_t w_{t,d}^2}}$$

quiz.question: Why use cosine similarity rather than dot product in VSM?
options: (1) All-or-nothing — no partial matching. (2) Query formulation burden on user.
VSM is a geometric model with no probabilistic justification.
Products of small probabilities underflow to zero numerically.
Dot product favours longer documents because they have larger magnitude vectors.
quiz.explanation: Dot product favours longer documents because they have larger magnitude vectors. Cosine normalises by vector magnitude, making similarity length-invariant. Score reflects angle, not magnitude.

quiz.question: What does a TF-IDF weight of 0 mean?
options: A document is "elite" for a term if the term is about the central topic of the document.
The query uses different words than the document. E.g., query = "heart attack", document = "myocardial infarction".
A retrieval model defines how to measure relevance between query and document.
Either TF=0 (term doesn't appear in the document) or IDF=0 (term appears in every document and is thus useless for discrimination).
quiz.explanation: Either TF=0 (term doesn't appear in the document) or IDF=0 (term appears in every document and is thus useless for discrimination). Both cases correctly give a weight of 0.

quiz.question: In VSM, how is a multi-term query represented?
options: IDF becomes negative — the term is so common it's anti-correlated with relevance.
(1) Vocabulary mismatch (no synonym handling). (2) All common terms get low IDF — the model degrades on queries with only high-frequency terms.
Parse into a query tree. Evaluate bottom-up.
As a vector where each dimension is the TF-IDF weight of the query term.
quiz.explanation: As a vector where each dimension is the TF-IDF weight of the query term. For single-occurrence terms in the query, TF=1, so weight = IDF(t).

quiz.question: What is the dimensionality of the VSM vector space?
options: The collection is pre-indexed; only the query varies.
An information need is the underlying intent ("I want to understand BM25 tuning").
BM25 is motivated by modelling term frequency as a mixture of two Poisson distributions: one for "elite" documents (topic-focused, higher TF) and one for "non-elite" documents.
|V| — the size of the vocabulary (number of unique terms).
quiz.explanation: |V| — the size of the vocabulary (number of unique terms). Typically 100K–1M for large corpora. Vectors are very sparse — most entries are 0.

quiz.question: Can cosine similarity distinguish two documents with identical term distributions but different lengths?
options: (1) Boolean model, (2) Vector Space Model (TF-IDF), (3) Probabilistic model (BM25, BIM), (4) Language Model (query likelihood), (5) Neural/Dense retrieval (bi-encoders).
BIM treats term occurrence as binary (0/1). BM25 adds: (1) term frequency (TF) component with saturation via k1, (2) document length normalisation via b.
IDF becomes negative — the term is so common it's anti-correlated with relevance.
No. Cosine similarity is length-invariant.
quiz.explanation: No. Cosine similarity is length-invariant. A 100-word doc and a 10,000-word doc with identical proportional TF will get the same cosine score.
